title: Why Loops Exist: Repetition Without Rewriting Code
learningObjectives: Explain why repeating instructions manually makes programs harder to maintain.
Describe a loop as a controlled way to repeat a block of instructions.
Identify the repeated action, changing value, and stopping condition in a simple loop.
Trace a small loop and predict how many times its body runs.
Recognize the risks of repetition without a correct stopping condition.

understand.concept: A loop repeats a set of instructions while a rule allows repetition or for a defined sequence of items. Without loops, repeated work often requires writing the same instruction many times. A loop can make repeated tasks shorter, easier to update, and less error-prone—but it must be controlled so it finishes when intended.
understand.whyItMatters: Programs frequently repeat tasks: processing a list of names, counting items, checking several records, retrying an operation, or drawing repeated shapes. Loops let one instruction handle many iterations instead of duplicating code.
understand.analogy: Imagine checking 30 packages at a warehouse. You could write 'check package 1', 'check package 2', and so on. A repeatable checklist process lets you perform the same steps for each package while keeping track of which one is next.
understand.analogyLimit: A loop is not simply an instruction to repeat forever. Programs need a clear rule, sequence, or stopping point; loops may also skip work or terminate early depending on their control flow.

explain.narrative: Repetition is a programming pattern in which the same action is performed multiple times. A loop usually has a loop body (the instructions being repeated), a control mechanism (such as a counter, condition, or collection), and a progress step that moves the process forward. The repeated work should be written once and applied on each iteration. Before using a loop, ask: what is repeated, what changes each time, and when should repetition stop? If progress never changes a condition that remains true, a loop may become infinite. Different languages provide different loop forms, but the central idea of controlled repetition is shared.

commonMistakes: Copying and pasting repeated instructions instead of using a loop.
Not identifying what should change between repetitions.
Using a stopping condition that is never reached.
Confusing one iteration with the whole loop.
Assuming every loop is guaranteed to run at least once.

Use a condition that allows the counter to reach 1.
Decrease the counter after each iteration.

independentTask.title: Independent: Repeat a useful action
independentTask.instructions: Write a small program that repeats a chosen action at least five times without duplicating the action statement.
requirements: Use a loop with a clear starting point or collection.
Choose and explain the stopping rule.
Show at least five outputs or processed items.
Describe one mistake that could cause unintended repetition.

The body contains the actions executed during each iteration.

questions.prompt: What helps a counter-controlled loop make progress?
options: Changing the counter on each iteration
questions.answer: Changing the counter on each iteration
questions.explanation: The update helps the loop reach its stopping condition.

questions.prompt: What is a possible result of a loop whose stopping condition never becomes false?
questions.explanation: If the termination condition stays true and no other exit occurs, the loop may not finish.

questions.prompt: Which question should you ask when designing repetition?
options: What repeats, what changes, and when does it stop?
How can I remove all conditions?
Can I copy the same statement more times?
questions.answer: What repeats, what changes, and when does it stop?
questions.explanation: These questions clarify the loop's repeated action, progress, and termination.
